title: Love the work (Avot 1:10)
hook: Shemaiah: love labor, hate lording over others, don't court the powerful

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon ben Shetach, the judge who knew a question can teach a lie. Your line was careful words. Did you ask one open question? Day two hundred forty-two.

A winter Friday in Jerusalem, a long time ago. A poor young laborer has spent half his day's wage to get into the house of study, and today he has nothing left, so the guard won't let him in. He climbs onto the roof and lies down by the skylight, just to hear the teachers talk. Snow begins to fall. He stays. In the morning, the two teachers inside notice the room is strangely dark. They look up and find a man buried in snow across the window. The Talmud says they carried him down, warmed him by the fire, and said he was worth it. The young man was Hillel. And one of his teachers was Shemaiah.
screen: `A WINTER FRIDAY.` → `HILLEL ON THE ROOF.` → `SHEMAIAH INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Shemaiah and his partner Avtalyon are the next pair in the chain of Pirkei Avot, and the Talmud remembers that they came from families of converts, yet they led the sages of their day. Shemaiah's saying has three short parts. First: love work. The Hebrew word is melakhah, the same word used for the creative work that stops on Shabbat. Not just tolerate your job. Love it. Many of the sages had trades. They were sandal makers, farmers, laborers, and they didn't see work as a distraction from a holy life. It was part of one. Second: hate rabbanut. It sounds like being a rabbi, but here it means lording it over people, holding a title so others have to bow. Shemaiah had authority, and he warns against loving it. Third: don't get too close to the ruling power. The rulers of his time could be dangerous, and later commentators say they draw you close when it suits them and drop you when it doesn't. Put the three together and you get a picture of a healthy life: honest work, done gladly, without climbing over people, and without selling yourself to whoever's in charge. Now go back to the roof. Hillel spent half of every wage just to be let in to learn. He loved the work, both kinds: the labor that paid the fee, and the learning it paid for. And the teachers who found him didn't hand him a title. They warmed him up.
screen: `SHEMAIAH AND AVTALYON.` · `LOVE WORK: MELAKHAH.` · `HATE LORDING IT OVER OTHERS.` · `DON'T COURT THE POWERFUL.` · then, large: `LOVE THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the part of your work you can love. Settle, and breathe. Picture a task waiting for you today: a report, a sink of dishes, a shift, homework. Don't picture the whole mountain. Find one small piece of it that's honestly good. The feel of a clean counter. A problem that clicks. A customer you helped. Hold that piece in your mind, and let yourself be glad of it. The bell holds the time.
Love the work. Shemaiah's teaching: honest labor done gladly, with no lording it over others and no chasing the powerful.
Your line: love the work. Today, do one ordinary task a little more carefully than you need to, and notice if it feels different. Day two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Many Jews read Avot 1:10 as a teaching about the dignity of work, and the sages of the Mishnah and Talmud are remembered as people with trades as well as teachers.

trapdoor: what it means: love honest labor, don't lord it over people, and don't sell yourself to the powerful.
what a scholar hears: melakhah is the same word the rabbis use for the kinds of creative work that stop on Shabbat.

notes: Hillel on the roof (Yoma 35b): half a tropaik to the guard, a winter Sabbath eve, snow over the skylight, warmed by the fire. The Talmud's line that he was worthy of having the Sabbath set aside for him is softened here to 'said he was worth it'; confirm.
Shemaiah and Avtalyon as descendants of converts: Yoma 71b and Gittin 57b; confirm.
'Sandal makers': Rabbi Yochanan the sandal-maker in Avot 4:11. 'Farmers, laborers' is a general statement; confirm it is fair.
The explanation of 'don't become intimate with the ruling power' draws on Avot 2:3; confirm.
